notes:
# Notes on 2 Thessalonians 3

**Sources and gaps.** I read four pages in full: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Gill's commentary on BibleHub, and the opening of the Precept Austin commentary, which cut off after v. 1. The rest of these notes come from search-result extracts of commentaries on BibleHub and StudyLight (Ellicott, Pulpit, Barnes, Calvin, Clarke, Bengel and others) and of articles on GotQuestions, GTY and catholic.com. What I couldn't find:
- **Lutheran and Pentecostal sources:** nothing specific to this chapter.
- **Orthodox sources:** nothing from oca.org. Chrysostom and Augustine only come up second-hand.
- **Modern scholarship:** nothing from bibleodyssey.org or the NET notes.
- **Prosperity, word of faith and hyper-grace teaching:** nothing on this chapter.

---

**v. 1**
- "Finally" doesn't necessarily mean the letter is ending. It can mean "for the rest" and marks a turn from doctrine to practical living. (MacArthur, quoted by Precept Austin) https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-thessalonians-3-commentary
- Paul often asked for prayer and believed his ministry's success partly depended on it. The request is for God's word to be free to work elsewhere as it had in Thessalonica. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/
- Gill takes "the word of the Lord" to mean the gospel. "Have free course" means "run," spreading far and wide, while Satan tries to block it. The word is "glorified" when people turn to Christ through it and believers live consistently with it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_thessalonians/3.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the wicked men were people trying to hinder the gospel. Paul wanted to be rescued from them, or for them to be changed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/
- Gill suggests either unbelieving Jews or false teachers. On "not everyone holds to the faith," he says faith is God's gift given only to the elect, which is a Reformed/Calvinist point. But he thinks the verse more likely means that not everyone who claims to believe actually does. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_thessalonians/3.htm

**v. 3**
- There's a contrast here: not all people have faith, but the Lord is faithful. God keeps Satan "on a leash" (1 Cor 10:13; Luke 22:31–32). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/
- Gill says the verse is there to comfort believers worried they might lose their faith. He teaches that true faith may weaken but will never finally fail, which is the Reformed doctrine of perseverance. The KJV has "keep you from evil." Gill applies this to the power of sin, to Satan the "evil one," and to evil people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_thessalonians/3.htm

**v. 4**
- God establishes believers partly by appealing to their wills: he works maturity in them "through our cooperation with His will." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/
- Paul's confidence rests on the Lord's strength, not on the Thessalonians themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_thessalonians/3.htm

**v. 5**
- The Greek verb pictures clearing a road of obstacles so the goal can be reached. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-thessalonians-3-commentary
- Love and endurance were what this church needed to stay stable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/
- "God's love" could mean our love for God or God's love for us. Gill sees the whole Trinity in the verse, with "the Lord" as the Spirit. "Christ's perseverance" has several possible senses:
  - Christ's own patience;
  - patience that Christ gives;
  - bearing the cross for him;
  - patiently waiting for his return (the KJV reading).
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_thessalonians/3.htm

**v. 6**
- **Traditional reading:**
  - "Disorderly" means not living by the apostles' pattern of teaching and life. The present tense shows a persistent habit (Hiebert). Withdrawing is meant to keep the offender from the comfort of fellowship until he repents, as in 1 Cor 5. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/
  - The word is a military image of soldiers out of rank. Ellicott says a "social excommunication rather than ecclesiastical seems chiefly meant." The Pulpit Commentary says there is "no allusion as yet to excommunication." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/3-6.htm
- **Differences on church government:** Gill, a Baptist, reads the verse as a command to the whole membership. In his view the power to exclude belongs to the congregation, not to pastors alone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_thessalonians/3.htm
- **Catholic vs Protestant on "tradition":**
  - Catholic: catholic.com uses this verse as evidence for binding apostolic Tradition beyond Scripture. https://www.catholic.com/tract/apostolic-tradition It also argues the NIV hides the word by translating it "teaching." https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-bible-and-other-traditions
  - Barnes: the word does not mean unwritten doctrines handed down from one person to another. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/3-6.htm
  - GTY (MacArthur) and GotQuestions: Paul means teaching the Thessalonians received directly from him, and nothing here shows it was preserved without error outside Scripture. https://www.gty.org/articles/A246/Scripture-Tradition-and-Rome-Part-3, https://www.gotquestions.org/Catholic-tradition.html
- Bengel used this verse against orders of begging friars (mendicant orders). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/3-6.htm

**vv. 7–9**
- Paul supported himself to set an example and to show he wasn't preaching for money, even though apostles had a right to support. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/

**v. 10**
- The key word is "unwilling," not "unable." https://www.gotquestions.org/2-Thessalonians-3-10-no-work-eat.html
- Barnes says it means not supported at public expense and was a Jewish proverb. Calvin says Paul isn't speaking to the idle but telling the church not to feed their laziness. Clarke, a Methodist, roots it in Genesis 3:19. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-thessalonians/3-10.html
- Bengel read it as a gentle joke: let the idler live without food like an angel. Others take it more simply as a penalty for idleness. One older comment notes it applies to the idle rich as well as the poor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/3-10.htm
- A BibleHub article says the verse is a church rule, not grounds for scrapping public safety nets, and condemns laziness, not poverty. It says the Didache and Chrysostom say the same. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_2_Thess_3_10_on_work_and_food.htm

**vv. 11–12**
- There is a play on words: "busybodies who do no business." Some may have thought Jesus' soon return made work pointless. Calvin aimed the verse at "our monks and priests." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/
- Augustine's treatise on the work of monks uses v. 12 as well. https://biblehub.com/study/2_thessalonians/3-10.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik reads this as encouragement not to let people who exploit generosity stop you from helping the truly needy. He quotes Spurgeon: doing good means faithfully doing everyday duties. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/
- Gill thought Paul added this so stingy people wouldn't use the instruction as an excuse to stop giving. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_thessalonians/3.htm

**v. 14**
- **How strong is the discipline?**
  - Ellicott: "note" means agreeing together to make him a marked man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/3-14.htm
  - Pulpit: shut him out of your fellowship meetings and love feasts. The aim is correction, not punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/3-14.htm
  - Geneva Bible notes (Reformed): this is excommunication. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/3-14.htm
  - Gill: formal exclusion, with the aim of bringing the person to repentance. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n95/2-thessalonians/3-14.html
- **A wording question:** Calvin attached "by this letter" to "note that man," meaning "report him to me in writing." The Pulpit Commentary prefers "our word in this letter." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-thessalonians-3.html

**v. 15**
- Calvin: the point of excommunication is to bring wanderers back, and it is distinct from anathema (a formal curse). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/

**v. 16**
- The peace comes from the Lord's own presence. Spurgeon stresses that the verse says the Lord himself gives peace, not through an angel or a minister. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/

**v. 17**
- Paul signed in his own hand to prove the letter was genuine and to guard against forged letters (compare 2:2). (Calvin, Constable, Matthew Henry) https://studylight.org/commentary/2-thessalonians/3-17.html
- **Modern scholarship:** some scholars argue a later follower of Paul wrote the letter, pointing to differences in style. The article I found, written from a conservative view, defends Paul's authorship from early manuscripts and church fathers. https://biblehub.com/q/why_debate_paul's_authorship_of_2_thess..htm

**v. 18**
- G. Campbell Morgan notes the word "all" is added compared with 1 Thessalonians, so the blessing includes even those Paul had just rebuked. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-3/
